context: process-led · kiln, mills & conveying dominate; refractory dry-out and staged loaded commissioning drive the back end

brief.intro: A cement plant is a heavy industrial process facility built around three huge rotating mechanical cores — the raw mill, the kiln (with its preheater tower and cooler), and the finish mill — tied together by kilometres of belt conveyors moving raw material, clinker and finished cement between them. Unlike a discrete-manufacturing plant, almost everything is oversized mechanical equipment and structural steel on massive concrete foundations: the kiln itself is a rotating steel tube tens of metres long, supported on piers, riding on tyres, and lined inside with refractory brick that must be dried out on a slow, controlled heat-up curve before it can ever see production temperature. Because the kiln, mills and conveyors are so large and long-lead, procurement of the major process equipment — kiln shell, preheater cyclones, mill bodies, conveyor drives — is what actually sets the schedule, even though the foundations for this equipment are themselves massive and early-critical. Commissioning is staged and cautious: individual machines run no-load first, then the whole material flow — quarry to crusher to raw mill to kiln to finish mill to dispatch — is proved loaded and slow, then ramped up to full rate, because taking a kiln from cold to full load in one step would damage the refractory lining.

scope.name: Enabling & site works
scope.desc: Earthworks, haul roads to the quarry/crusher, site utilities.

scope.name: Civil & heavy equipment foundations
scope.desc: Kiln piers, mill bases, preheater tower base and other mass-concrete foundations, cast to tight tolerance.

scope.name: Structural steel & silos
scope.desc: Preheater tower, conveyor galleries, transfer towers, and clinker/cement silo shells.

scope.name: Process equipment — crushing & grinding
scope.desc: Crusher, raw mill and finish mill bodies, set and aligned on their foundations.

scope.name: Kiln & pyroprocessing
scope.desc: Kiln shell assembly, preheater cyclones, cooler, refractory lining and controlled dry-out.

scope.name: Material handling / conveying
scope.desc: Belt conveyors, bucket elevators, stackers and reclaimers linking every process step.

scope.name: Electrical & drives
scope.desc: MV/LV switchgear, motor control centres and variable-speed drives for the large rotating equipment.

scope.name: Instrumentation & control
scope.desc: Weigh feeders, level/flow/temperature instrumentation and the Distributed Control System (DCS).

scope.name: Dust collection & environmental
scope.desc: Baghouses and dust collectors protecting the stack emissions at every transfer point.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: No-load runs, refractory dry-out, loaded material-flow proving and ramp-up to full rate.

glossary.plain: the intermediate product made by burning raw meal in the kiln — ground with gypsum afterward to make finished cement.
the long rotating steel tube, lined with refractory, where raw meal is heated to around 1450°C to form clinker.
a tall stack of cyclones that pre-heats raw meal with hot kiln exhaust gas before it enters the kiln, saving fuel.
the heat-resistant brick or castable lining inside the kiln and preheater, which must be slowly dried out before production temperature.
the large rotating mills that grind raw materials into "raw meal" before the kiln, and clinker plus gypsum into finished cement after it.
an instrumented conveyor that doses material by weight rather than volume — critical to getting the raw-mix recipe right.
a large fabric-filter dust collector that captures kiln and mill exhaust dust before it reaches the stack.
staged commissioning steps — first running equipment empty to prove mechanical function, then progressively loaded with material.

must_get_right: Order the kiln shell, preheater cyclones and mill bodies first — their fabrication and delivery lead time, not the civil works, is what actually sets the completion date.
Get the heavy equipment foundations (kiln piers, mill bases) right and early — they are cast to tight tolerance and cannot be revisited once the kiln or mill is set.
Protect the refractory dry-out and controlled heat-up curve at the end of the programme — rushing it damages the lining and can cost weeks of kiln downtime to repair.
Sequence commissioning as a staged material-flow proving (no-load → loaded → full rate) from quarry to dispatch, not as a single plant-wide switch-on.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil works and structural steel run a 6-day week; heavy equipment set (kiln, mills, crushers) moves to two shifts to protect the erection window; refractory dry-out runs a continuous 24/7 calendar once started, since the heat-up curve cannot be paused without damaging the lining; commissioning and ramp-up also run 24/7.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs kiln shell / preheater / mill procurement → heavy equipment foundations → structural steel & silo erection → equipment set & align → refractory installation → controlled dry-out / heat-up → no-load then loaded material-flow proving → full-rate performance test. Civil works away from the kiln and mill foundations are rarely critical once those foundations are cast; the equipment procurement chain and the refractory dry-out own the back end of the schedule.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Process design and equipment guarantees are frozen before the kiln, mill and crusher packages are ordered; a single mobilisation; quarry and raw-material supply are established ahead of commissioning; grid power connection is available before drive commissioning starts.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy-lift crane windows are needed for kiln sections, mill shells and preheater cyclones; specialist refractory installation and dry-out engineers are a constrained resource late in the programme; commissioning needs the raw-material feed chain (quarry, crusher, raw mill) proven before kiln first-fire.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: kiln or mill package delivery slippage, refractory dry-out extension from weather or lining defects, and interruptions during the loaded ramp-up. Schedule contingency is held before the refractory dry-out and before the loaded ramp-up rather than spread across civil and structural steel.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
